statements.quote: Concretely, an **AI Agent** is a system where a Large Language Model acts not merely as a text generator, but as a **controller inside an observe→reason→act loop**.
It can be given access to its environment (a file system, a browser, an API), reason about which tool to invoke, observe the result, and iterate until a task is complete.
The LLM remains the “decision-making component” of a loop rather than a one-shot oracle.

The difference between “using an LLM” and “deploying an agent” is the difference between asking someone a question (in their head) and hiring them to complete a project (with hands on a keyboard, a browser, a terminal).
The hired person's *cognitive architecture* has not changed; what changed is the set of effectors available to them.
The same is true of the LLM inside an agent.
The “Re” in **ReAct** is the reasoning loop from the Reasoning chapter ; the “Act” is just a tool call appended to each reasoning step.
Everything in this chapter assumes familiarity with CoT, self-consistency, and verification-guided search.
The concept of an autonomous reasoning agent long predates LLMs.
statements.section: Historical Roots: Where Did the Idea Come From?

statements.quote: Understanding the lineage helps explain why modern agents work the way they do.
statements.section: Historical Roots: Where Did the Idea Come From?

statements.quote: The deepest historical root of the modern AI agent is not from AI research at all but from a *psychology*-oriented network engineer asking what computers were actually *for*.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: \citeauthor{licklider1960symbiosis} (\citeyear{licklider1960symbiosis}) published "Man-Computer Symbiosis" in the IRE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics while at Bolt, Beranek and Newman, two years before he took charge of ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, where he funded the time-sharing and networking research that led to the ARPANET and helped shape what became the internet.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The paper argues, against the prevailing orthodoxy of the day (which held that computers would automate human decision-making by replacing humans), that the right relation between human and computer is not *replacement* but *symbiosis* — a tight, real-time, two-way coupling in which each partner does what it does best.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The hope is that, in not too many years, human brains and computing machines will be coupled together very tightly, and that the resulting partnership will think as no human brain has ever thought and process data in a way not approached by the information-handling machines we know today.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The paper's bet is that *men* and *computers* are complementary, not competing: humans set the goals, anticipate, evaluate, and supply the ethical and aesthetic frame; computers do the routinizable clerical, bookkeeping, and search work.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The interaction is **time-sharing** (one computer, many simultaneous human partners), **interactive** (the computer responds within seconds to the human's query), and **cooperative** (the human and the computer iterate toward a goal).
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The paper's time-and-motion study of his own technical work found that most “thinking” time went into clerical and mechanical operations — searching, calculating, plotting, transforming, and tracing logical consequences — which map onto what a modern LLM agent does with tools:
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: Read sixty-five years later, \citeauthor{licklider1960symbiosis}'s *man-computer symbiosis* is a one-paragraph specification for the modern AI agent.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: He even predicts the cooperative architecture from first principles: the human handles "the creative thinking" — goals, evaluation, judgement; the machine handles "the routine work" — bookkeeping, search, mechanical inference; the partnership iterates in real time.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The only thing \citeauthor{licklider1960symbiosis} got wrong was timing — he predicted it would happen "in not too many years" from 1960, and it actually happened in roughly 2022, once the LLM that could *reason about which tool to call* arrived.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The LLM is the long-expected *seam* between the human's question and the computer's action that Licklider's essay was describing.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The historical line from Licklider to the present agent loop runs through infrastructure he helped fund and imagine: time-sharing (MIT's CTSS was running by 1961, and Licklider funded Project MAC from 1963), packet-switched networking (the ARPANET, built in 1969 by others on the institutional groundwork he laid, and later the internet), and finally the natural-language interface — not restricted command grammars like SHRDLU's blocks world, but a general interface that could map open-ended English onto arbitrary tools, which is what LLMs supplied.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: When the LLM arrived, every precondition for the symbiosis was already in place; all that was missing was the *natural-language seam*, and the seam is the agent.
statements.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

statements.quote: The earliest AI agents were purely symbolic.
\cite[McCarthy and Hayes (1969)]{mccarthy1969some} formalized the **frame problem**, how an agent reasons about what changes and what stays the same when it acts.
The dominant paradigm was **GOFAI** (Good Old-Fashioned AI): hand-coded rules, planning algorithms, and explicit world models.

GPS (General Problem Solver) 1957 Means-ends analysis: reduce difference between current and goal state STRIPS 1971 Formal action schemas with preconditions and effects SHRDLU 1972 Natural language commands to manipulate a blocks world Soar 1983 Universal cognitive architecture with chunking and learning BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) 1995 Agents with explicit beliefs, desires, and committed intentions (after Bratman's 1987 theory)
\citealternativetitle{shrdlu_image}.

Terry Winograd's SHRDLU (1972) let a user type English sentences (“pick up a big red block”) to manipulate a virtual world of colored blocks, the canonical demonstration that natural-language reasoning over a small world was possible.
These systems were brittle: they required complete world models and broke on ambiguity.
But they established the **observe → reason → act** loop that modern agents inherit.
This gave us game-playing agents (TD-Gammon, AlphaGo), but they were trained for one game at a time, needed enormous experience, and could not carry their skill into a new task.
\citealternativetitle{alphago_leesedol_image}: world champion Lee Sedol (right) studies the board as Aja Huang (left) places stones on behalf of AlphaGo during Game 4, March 2016 in Seoul.
AlphaGo won the match 4–1 and became the first program to defeat a top human player at Go.
The breakthrough insight, articulated in (\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023react}), was that LLMs already encode vast world knowledge and can perform multi-step reasoning in natural language.
Instead of learning a policy from scratch, you can use the LLM *as* the policy, prompting it to reason, select tools, and iterate.
This collapses the classical agent architecture into a single model that handles perception (reading text), reasoning (chain-of-thought), and action selection (tool calls) simultaneously.
The most influential framework for LLM agents is **ReAct** (\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023react}), which interleaves **Re**asoning traces and **Act**ions in a single prompt stream:
The key innovation is that **Thought** and **Action** alternate in the same token stream.
The LLM generates both its internal reasoning *and* its tool calls as text.
The orchestrator parses the actions, executes them, and injects the observations back into the context.
\cite[Yao et al. (2023)]{yao2023react} showed that:
- **Reasoning without acting** (chain-of-thought alone) hallucinates facts it cannot verify.
- **Acting without reasoning** (tool use without explicit thought) makes incoherent tool choices.
- **ReAct** (both together) achieves the best of both worlds: grounded, interpretable, multi-step problem solving.
SHRDLU was a high-water mark of the early symbolic approach.

Terry Winograd's program parsed English commands, planned in a blocks world, and answered questions about its own actions; it was a genuine natural-language system, but only inside a hand-built microworld whose vocabulary, planner, and objects were all fixed \cite{winograd1972understanding}.

A decade later Rodney Brooks drew the opposite lesson: his subsumption architecture built robots from layers of simple reactive behaviours, each suppressing the one below, with no central world model and no planner \cite{brooks1986layered}.
“Elephants Don't Play Chess” added the slogan — the world is its own best model \cite{brooks1990elephants}.
In parallel with robotics, cognitive science built unified architectures.
Soar modelled problem solving as search through a problem space, with impasses triggering subgoals and “chunking” compiling the result of a subgoal into a new rule \cite{laird1987soar}.
ACT-R partitioned cognition into modules — declarative memory, production rules, buffers — and calibrated their timing against human behaviour \cite{anderson2004actr}.
The BDI tradition gave agents an explicit practical-reasoning vocabulary: beliefs model the world, desires are goals, and intentions are the goals the agent has committed to pursue \cite{rao1995bdi}.
The modern LLM agent's scratchpad, memory store, and control loop are a loose, learned reimplementation of this functional list.
ReAct taught a model to call tools in its text; Toolformer asked whether a model could learn when to call them.

Schick et al. let GPT-J annotate its own corpus by trying API calls — a calculator, a search engine, a translator — and kept only calls whose result lowered the model's perplexity on the following tokens, then fine-tuned on that self-labelled data \cite{schick2023toolformer}.
The model learned to insert calls without being told which calls were useful.
Toolformer is the bridge between prompt-level ReAct and today's function-calling APIs: both make tool use a learned, token-level decision rather than an external orchestration rule.
Every LLM agent, regardless of framework, implements a variant of this loop:
Read user goal + conversation history Read observations from previous tool calls Read working memory / scratchpad
System prompt sets persona, tools & constraints LLM generates chain-of-thought Decides: done, or which tool?
If done → emit final answer If not → emit structured tool call Orchestrator validates request
Tool executes in sandbox Result injected as “Observation” Loop back to PERCEIVE
LLM emits a “Finish” action Maximum iterations reached (safety bound) Token budget exhausted Error threshold exceeded
Concrete coding agents implement this loop as **multi-step tool usage**.

A deep dive into the opencode agent (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}) shows the pattern clearly: the LLM call is a streaming loop in which the model continuously emits text and tool calls, the framework executes each call, and the results are fed back into the context.
Termination is explicit — a `stopWhen` clause ends the loop after a maximum number of steps, and a rejected permission request aborts it.
The framework processes the stream event by event (text deltas, tool calls, tool results, tool errors), persisting each artifact to disk as it goes.
This is precisely the observe→reason→act cycle of the diagram above, made concrete.

statements.quote: Tool use (also called **function calling**) is the bridge between the LLM's text world and the real world.
statements.section: Tool Use: The Mechanism in Detail

statements.quote: The mechanism works identically to what was described in the web search chapter, but generalized to arbitrary tools.
statements.section: Tool Use: The Mechanism in Detail

statements.quote: The LLM doesn't execute anything.
It generates a **structured text output** that the orchestrator parses and executes:
Tools are defined as JSON schemas that the LLM sees in its system prompt:
Real registries look exactly like this.

The opencode agent ships a set of built-in tools — read, write, edit, bash, glob, grep, list, webfetch, todo management, and a task tool for spawning sub-agents — each defined with a description and a parameters schema and registered so the model can invoke it by name (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}).
The description and schema are what the LLM sees; an `execute` function is what actually runs when the model decides to call the tool.

The same function-calling primitives are used with every major provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), because a provider-agnostic SDK translates the tool definitions into each vendor's dialect.
A single LLM call is stateless, it only “remembers” what's in its context window.
Agents need memory to handle multi-step tasks that span many interactions.
Memory Type Mechanism Analogy

Working Memory The current context window contents Your desk right now Short-term Memory Conversation history (recent turns) What was said 5 minutes ago Long-term Memory External vector database (RAG) Your filing cabinet Episodic Memory Logs of past agent runs Your diary Procedural Memory Learned tool-use patterns (fine-tuning) Muscle memory

A practical illustration of session-scoped working memory comes from the opencode agent: it exposes todo-list tools (write and read) whose state persists per session and is fed back into the model — an explicit prompt-level scratchpad (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}).
And when the growing conversation history approaches the model's context limit, the agent automatically summarizes the session so far and continues from that summary instead of losing state entirely.
Many agent frameworks give the LLM a **scratchpad**, a section of the prompt where it can write intermediate results that persist across iterations:
A single agent has limits: context window size, expertise breadth, and the tendency to lose focus on long tasks.
**Multi-agent systems** address this by having multiple specialized agents collaborate.
Pattern Description Example

Hierarchical A “manager” agent delegates subtasks to “worker” agents CEO agent assigns research to analyst agent, writing to editor agent Debate Multiple agents argue different positions, a judge synthesizes Red team vs. blue team for security analysis Pipeline Agents process sequentially, each refining the previous output Researcher → Writer → Editor → Fact-checker Swarm Agents work in parallel on independent subtasks, results merged Multiple search agents covering different aspects of a question
Agents communicate through the same mechanism as tool use, one agent's output becomes another agent's input, mediated by an orchestrator:
In practice, sub-agents are often just another tool.

The opencode agent, for example, exposes a single `task` tool whose description enumerates the available sub-agents; invoking it spins up a brand-new session with its own context window, its own toolset, and possibly a different model, and the sub-agent's final output is returned as the tool result (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}).
The orchestrator in the diagram above can therefore be another LLM — a recursive delegation that hints at full autonomy.
The 2023 autonomous-agent wave turned ReAct into a product.
statements.section: AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems

statements.quote: AutoGPT, released in March 2023, gave GPT-4 a goal, a set of tools, and a loop that decomposed the goal into tasks, executed them, and wrote results to memory; it went viral as the first widely seen “fully autonomous” agent, though in practice it often looped, drifted, or burned tokens \cite{autogpt2023}.

statements.quote: Voyager went the other way, embedding an LLM agent in Minecraft with an automatic curriculum and a skill library, so that successful programs could be stored and reused \cite{wang2023voyager}.

statements.quote: Naive agents attempt tasks step-by-step without foresight.
statements.section: Planning: How Agents Decompose Complex Tasks

statements.quote: More sophisticated agents **plan** before acting, decomposing complex goals into subtasks.
statements.section: Planning: How Agents Decompose Complex Tasks

statements.quote: The agent first generates a complete plan, then executes each step; plan-and-solve prompting showed that asking a model to plan before solving improves zero-shot reasoning (\cite[Wang et al., 2023]{wang2023planandexecute}):
\cite[Reflexion]{shinn2023reflexion} adds a self-evaluation step: after completing a task, the agent reflects on what went wrong and stores that reflection in memory for future attempts.
An agent that can act on the world (send emails, execute code, make purchases) must be **grounded**, its actions must correspond to the user's actual intent.
Misalignment between the user's goal and the agent's interpretation can cause real harm.

Goal misinterpretation “Clean up my inbox” → agent deletes all emails Confirmation steps for destructive actions Reward hacking Agent finds shortcuts that satisfy metrics but not intent Human-in-the-loop checkpoints Unbounded iteration Agent enters infinite loop trying to achieve impossible goal Maximum iteration limits Tool misuse Agent uses code execution to access unauthorized resources Sandboxing, permission systems Prompt injection via tools Malicious content in web search results hijacks agent Input sanitization, instruction hierarchy
Every safety measure (confirmations, sandboxing, human review) adds latency and reduces autonomy.
This creates a fundamental tension:
The field is actively researching how to push this frontier, making agents both more capable *and* more aligned simultaneously, rather than trading one for the other.
Concrete agents build these mitigations in from the start.

In opencode (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}), a permission system gates sensitive tools like `bash`, so a read-only planning agent must explicitly request approval before executing anything; the read tool refuses binary files, and edits are rejected for paths outside the working directory; oversized tool output is truncated before it re-enters the context; and at each step the agent records a git snapshot of the working tree, letting a failed change be rolled back in full.

One grounding mechanism deserves special mention: after the model edits a file, the agent queries a Language Server for static diagnostics and feeds them back into the context, so undefined symbols or type errors become immediately visible — a squiggly-line IDE check injected into the agent's own observations.
The same loop that makes an agent useful makes it a reusable attack harness.
Replace the user's goal with network discovery and the tools with a shell, and the observe-reason-act cycle becomes a way to probe a host, read the result, and try again.

\cite[Guan et al. (2026)]{guan2026adaptiveworms} built a proof-of-concept worm around exactly this architecture: a phase-structured agent core, a hierarchical memory, and a tool layer for shell sessions and file transfer, all driven by a single-GPU open-weight LLM hosted on a compromised machine.
Once a host was taken, a copy of the agent was staged there and pointed at the next target, so the attack scaled without a human operator.
This is why an agent's tool permissions, network reach, and ability to write and execute code are security boundaries, not convenience settings.
The agent paradigm has spawned numerous open-source frameworks:
Framework Language Key Feature

LangChain / LangGraph Python Graph-based agent workflows with state machines AutoGPT Python Fully autonomous goal-pursuing agent (2023 viral demo) CrewAI Python Multi-agent role-based collaboration Microsoft AutoGen Python Conversational multi-agent framework Semantic Kernel C# / Python Microsoft's enterprise agent SDK OpenAI Assistants API API Managed agent infrastructure with built-in tools Anthropic Claude Tool Use API Native function calling with safety constraints opencode TypeScript / Bun Open-source coding agent: client/server architecture (Hono HTTP server + Go terminal UI), provider-agnostic through the AI SDK (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}) Neuron (PHP) PHP Agent framework for PHP backend engineers
All of these implement the same core loop described above, they differ in how they manage state, compose tools, handle errors, and coordinate multiple agents.

The LLM is the long-expected *seam* between the human's question and the computer's action that Licklider's essay was describing.
blocks.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

blocks.quote: The historical line from Licklider to the present agent loop runs through infrastructure he helped fund and imagine: time-sharing (MIT's CTSS was running by 1961, and Licklider funded Project MAC from 1963), packet-switched networking (the ARPANET, built in 1969 by others on the institutional groundwork he laid, and later the internet), and finally the natural-language interface — not restricted command grammars like SHRDLU's blocks world, but a general interface that could map open-ended English onto arbitrary tools, which is what LLMs supplied. When the LLM arrived, every precondition for the symbiosis was already in place; all that was missing was the *natural-language seam*, and the seam is the agent.
blocks.section: 0. Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960) — the Vision Before the Tech

blocks.quote: 1. Classical AI: Symbolic Agents (1950s–1990s)

The earliest AI agents were purely symbolic. \cite[McCarthy and Hayes (1969)]{mccarthy1969some} formalized the **frame problem**, how an agent reasons about what changes and what stays the same when it acts. The dominant paradigm was **GOFAI** (Good Old-Fashioned AI): hand-coded rules, planning algorithms, and explicit world models.
System Year Key Idea

GPS (General Problem Solver) 1957 Means-ends analysis: reduce difference between current and goal state STRIPS 1971 Formal action schemas with preconditions and effects SHRDLU 1972 Natural language commands to manipulate a blocks world Soar 1983 Universal cognitive architecture with chunking and learning BDI (Belief-Desire-Intention) 1995 Agents with explicit beliefs, desires, and committed intentions (after Bratman's 1987 theory)

\citealternativetitle{shrdlu_image}. Terry Winograd's SHRDLU (1972) let a user type English sentences (“pick up a big red block”) to manipulate a virtual world of colored blocks, the canonical demonstration that natural-language reasoning over a small world was possible.
These systems were brittle: they required complete world models and broke on ambiguity. But they established the **observe → reason → act** loop that modern agents inherit.
2. Reinforcement Learning Agents (1990s–2010s)
This gave us game-playing agents (TD-Gammon, AlphaGo), but they were trained for one game at a time, needed enormous experience, and could not carry their skill into a new task.

\citealternativetitle{alphago_leesedol_image}: world champion Lee Sedol (right) studies the board as Aja Huang (left) places stones on behalf of AlphaGo during Game 4, March 2016 in Seoul. AlphaGo won the match 4–1 and became the first program to defeat a top human player at Go.
3. The LLM Agent Revolution (2022–present)

The breakthrough insight, articulated in (\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023react}), was that LLMs already encode vast world knowledge and can perform multi-step reasoning in natural language. Instead of learning a policy from scratch, you can use the LLM *as* the policy, prompting it to reason, select tools, and iterate.
This collapses the classical agent architecture into a single model that handles perception (reading text), reasoning (chain-of-thought), and action selection (tool calls) simultaneously.
The ReAct Paradigm: Reasoning + Acting
The most influential framework for LLM agents is **ReAct** (\cite[Yao et al., 2023]{yao2023react}), which interleaves **Re**asoning traces and **Act**ions in a single prompt stream:

The key innovation is that **Thought** and **Action** alternate in the same token stream. The LLM generates both its internal reasoning *and* its tool calls as text. The orchestrator parses the actions, executes them, and injects the observations back into the context.
Why interleaving matters
\cite[Yao et al. (2023)]{yao2023react} showed that:
- **Reasoning without acting** (chain-of-thought alone) hallucinates facts it cannot verify.
- **Acting without reasoning** (tool use without explicit thought) makes incoherent tool choices.
- **ReAct** (both together) achieves the best of both worlds: grounded, interpretable, multi-step problem solving.
SHRDLU and the architecture tradition

SHRDLU was a high-water mark of the early symbolic approach. Terry Winograd's program parsed English commands, planned in a blocks world, and answered questions about its own actions; it was a genuine natural-language system, but only inside a hand-built microworld whose vocabulary, planner, and objects were all fixed \cite{winograd1972understanding}. A decade later Rodney Brooks drew the opposite lesson: his subsumption architecture built robots from layers of simple reactive behaviours, each suppressing the one below, with no central world model and no planner \cite{brooks1986layered}. “Elephants Don't Play Chess” added the slogan — the world is its own best model \cite{brooks1990elephants}.

In parallel with robotics, cognitive science built unified architectures. Soar modelled problem solving as search through a problem space, with impasses triggering subgoals and “chunking” compiling the result of a subgoal into a new rule \cite{laird1987soar}. ACT-R partitioned cognition into modules — declarative memory, production rules, buffers — and calibrated their timing against human behaviour \cite{anderson2004actr}. The BDI tradition gave agents an explicit practical-reasoning vocabulary: beliefs model the world, desires are goals, and intentions are the goals the agent has committed to pursue \cite{rao1995bdi}. The modern LLM agent's scratchpad, memory store, and control loop are a loose, learned reimplementation of this functional list.
Toolformer: learning when to call

ReAct taught a model to call tools in its text; Toolformer asked whether a model could learn when to call them. Schick et al. let GPT-J annotate its own corpus by trying API calls — a calculator, a search engine, a translator — and kept only calls whose result lowered the model's perplexity on the following tokens, then fine-tuned on that self-labelled data \cite{schick2023toolformer}. The model learned to insert calls without being told which calls were useful. Toolformer is the bridge between prompt-level ReAct and today's function-calling APIs: both make tool use a learned, token-level decision rather than an external orchestration rule.
The Agent Loop: Internal Architecture
Every LLM agent, regardless of framework, implements a variant of this loop:
The Agent Loop
1 PERCEIVE
Read user goal + conversation history Read observations from previous tool calls Read working memory / scratchpad
2 REASON
System prompt sets persona, tools & constraints LLM generates chain-of-thought Decides: done, or which tool?
3 ACT
If done → emit final answer If not → emit structured tool call Orchestrator validates request
4 OBSERVE
Tool executes in sandbox Result injected as “Observation” Loop back to PERCEIVE
Termination Conditions
LLM emits a “Finish” action Maximum iterations reached (safety bound) Token budget exhausted Error threshold exceeded

Concrete coding agents implement this loop as **multi-step tool usage**. A deep dive into the opencode agent (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}) shows the pattern clearly: the LLM call is a streaming loop in which the model continuously emits text and tool calls, the framework executes each call, and the results are fed back into the context. Termination is explicit — a `stopWhen` clause ends the loop after a maximum number of steps, and a rejected permission request aborts it. The framework processes the stream event by event (text deltas, tool calls, tool results, tool errors), persisting each artifact to disk as it goes. This is precisely the observe→reason→act cycle of the diagram above, made concrete.

In opencode, the effective system prompt is assembled at runtime from several sources — a provider-specific base prompt, an optional `AGENTS.md` file from the project, and an agent-specific prompt — and switching between a read-only planning mode and a full build mode is itself injected as a system reminder (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}).

blocks.quote: Tool Use: The Mechanism in Detail
blocks.section: Tool Use: The Mechanism in Detail

blocks.quote: Tool use (also called **function calling**) is the bridge between the LLM's text world and the real world. The mechanism works identically to what was described in the web search chapter, but generalized to arbitrary tools.
blocks.section: Tool Use: The Mechanism in Detail

blocks.quote: How the LLM “calls” a tool
The LLM doesn't execute anything. It generates a **structured text output** that the orchestrator parses and executes:
The Tool Registry
Tools are defined as JSON schemas that the LLM sees in its system prompt:

Real registries look exactly like this. The opencode agent ships a set of built-in tools — read, write, edit, bash, glob, grep, list, webfetch, todo management, and a task tool for spawning sub-agents — each defined with a description and a parameters schema and registered so the model can invoke it by name (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}). The description and schema are what the LLM sees; an `execute` function is what actually runs when the model decides to call the tool. The same function-calling primitives are used with every major provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), because a provider-agnostic SDK translates the tool definitions into each vendor's dialect.
Memory: How Agents Remember
A single LLM call is stateless, it only “remembers” what's in its context window. Agents need memory to handle multi-step tasks that span many interactions.
Types of Agent Memory
Memory Type Mechanism Analogy

Working Memory The current context window contents Your desk right now Short-term Memory Conversation history (recent turns) What was said 5 minutes ago Long-term Memory External vector database (RAG) Your filing cabinet Episodic Memory Logs of past agent runs Your diary Procedural Memory Learned tool-use patterns (fine-tuning) Muscle memory

A practical illustration of session-scoped working memory comes from the opencode agent: it exposes todo-list tools (write and read) whose state persists per session and is fed back into the model — an explicit prompt-level scratchpad (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}). And when the growing conversation history approaches the model's context limit, the agent automatically summarizes the session so far and continues from that summary instead of losing state entirely.
The Scratchpad Pattern
Many agent frameworks give the LLM a **scratchpad**, a section of the prompt where it can write intermediate results that persist across iterations:
Multi-Agent Systems

A single agent has limits: context window size, expertise breadth, and the tendency to lose focus on long tasks. **Multi-agent systems** address this by having multiple specialized agents collaborate.
Architectures
Pattern Description Example

Hierarchical A “manager” agent delegates subtasks to “worker” agents CEO agent assigns research to analyst agent, writing to editor agent Debate Multiple agents argue different positions, a judge synthesizes Red team vs. blue team for security analysis Pipeline Agents process sequentially, each refining the previous output Researcher → Writer → Editor → Fact-checker Swarm Agents work in parallel on independent subtasks, results merged Multiple search agents covering different aspects of a question
Communication Between Agents
Agents communicate through the same mechanism as tool use, one agent's output becomes another agent's input, mediated by an orchestrator:

In practice, sub-agents are often just another tool. The opencode agent, for example, exposes a single `task` tool whose description enumerates the available sub-agents; invoking it spins up a brand-new session with its own context window, its own toolset, and possibly a different model, and the sub-agent's final output is returned as the tool result (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}). The orchestrator in the diagram above can therefore be another LLM — a recursive delegation that hints at full autonomy.
AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems
blocks.section: AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems

blocks.quote: The 2023 autonomous-agent wave turned ReAct into a product. AutoGPT, released in March 2023, gave GPT-4 a goal, a set of tools, and a loop that decomposed the goal into tasks, executed them, and wrote results to memory; it went viral as the first widely seen “fully autonomous” agent, though in practice it often looped, drifted, or burned tokens \cite{autogpt2023}. Voyager went the other way, embedding an LLM agent in Minecraft with an automatic curriculum and a skill library, so that successful programs could be stored and reused \cite{wang2023voyager}.
blocks.section: AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems

blocks.quote: For years every agent framework invented its own tool schema. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), announced by Anthropic in November 2024, tried to standardise the interface: an MCP server exposes resources, prompts, and tools over JSON-RPC, and any MCP-capable client can discover and call them \cite{anthropic2024mcp}. The design separates the tool provider from the agent runtime, so a database, a file system, or a SaaS product can be written once and used by many agents.
blocks.section: AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems

blocks.quote: Multi-agent systems are older than LLMs: blackboard architectures, contract-net protocols, and BDI teams were studied through the 1980s and 1990s. The LLM version keeps the coordination patterns but replaces hand-written protocols with natural-language messages. Du et al. showed that several model instances debating across rounds can improve factuality and reasoning over a single pass \cite{du2023multiagent}, while AutoGen framed the whole application as a conversation between configurable agents \cite{wu2023autogen}. The open question is whether the gains come from genuine division of labour or simply from more samples and more test-time compute.
blocks.section: AutoGPT, Voyager, MCP, and multi-agent systems

blocks.section: Planning: How Agents Decompose Complex Tasks

blocks.quote: Naive agents attempt tasks step-by-step without foresight. More sophisticated agents **plan** before acting, decomposing complex goals into subtasks.
blocks.section: Planning: How Agents Decompose Complex Tasks

blocks.quote: Plan-and-Execute

The agent first generates a complete plan, then executes each step; plan-and-solve prompting showed that asking a model to plan before solving improves zero-shot reasoning (\cite[Wang et al., 2023]{wang2023planandexecute}):
Reflexion: Learning from Mistakes
\cite[Reflexion]{shinn2023reflexion} adds a self-evaluation step: after completing a task, the agent reflects on what went wrong and stores that reflection in memory for future attempts.
Grounding and Safety: The Hard Problems
blocks.section: Grounding and Safety: The Hard Problems

blocks.quote: The Grounding Problem

An agent that can act on the world (send emails, execute code, make purchases) must be **grounded**, its actions must correspond to the user's actual intent. Misalignment between the user's goal and the agent's interpretation can cause real harm.
Risk Example Mitigation

Goal misinterpretation “Clean up my inbox” → agent deletes all emails Confirmation steps for destructive actions Reward hacking Agent finds shortcuts that satisfy metrics but not intent Human-in-the-loop checkpoints Unbounded iteration Agent enters infinite loop trying to achieve impossible goal Maximum iteration limits Tool misuse Agent uses code execution to access unauthorized resources Sandboxing, permission systems Prompt injection via tools Malicious content in web search results hijacks agent Input sanitization, instruction hierarchy
The Autonomy–Safety Trade-off
Every safety measure (confirmations, sandboxing, human review) adds latency and reduces autonomy. This creates a fundamental tension:
The field is actively researching how to push this frontier, making agents both more capable *and* more aligned simultaneously, rather than trading one for the other.

Concrete agents build these mitigations in from the start. In opencode (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}), a permission system gates sensitive tools like `bash`, so a read-only planning agent must explicitly request approval before executing anything; the read tool refuses binary files, and edits are rejected for paths outside the working directory; oversized tool output is truncated before it re-enters the context; and at each step the agent records a git snapshot of the working tree, letting a failed change be rolled back in full. One grounding mechanism deserves special mention: after the model edits a file, the agent queries a Language Server for static diagnostics and feeds them back into the context, so undefined symbols or type errors become immediately visible — a squiggly-line IDE check injected into the agent's own observations.
Agents as Attack Infrastructure

The same loop that makes an agent useful makes it a reusable attack harness. Replace the user's goal with network discovery and the tools with a shell, and the observe-reason-act cycle becomes a way to probe a host, read the result, and try again. \cite[Guan et al. (2026)]{guan2026adaptiveworms} built a proof-of-concept worm around exactly this architecture: a phase-structured agent core, a hierarchical memory, and a tool layer for shell sessions and file transfer, all driven by a single-GPU open-weight LLM hosted on a compromised machine. Once a host was taken, a copy of the agent was staged there and pointed at the next target, so the attack scaled without a human operator. This is why an agent's tool permissions, network reach, and ability to write and execute code are security boundaries, not convenience settings.
Frameworks and Implementations
The agent paradigm has spawned numerous open-source frameworks:
Framework Language Key Feature

LangChain / LangGraph Python Graph-based agent workflows with state machines AutoGPT Python Fully autonomous goal-pursuing agent (2023 viral demo) CrewAI Python Multi-agent role-based collaboration Microsoft AutoGen Python Conversational multi-agent framework Semantic Kernel C# / Python Microsoft's enterprise agent SDK OpenAI Assistants API API Managed agent infrastructure with built-in tools Anthropic Claude Tool Use API Native function calling with safety constraints opencode TypeScript / Bun Open-source coding agent: client/server architecture (Hono HTTP server + Go terminal UI), provider-agnostic through the AI SDK (\cite[Abboud, 2025]{abboud2025opencode}) Neuron (PHP) PHP Agent framework for PHP backend engineers
All of these implement the same core loop described above, they differ in how they manage state, compose tools, handle errors, and coordinate multiple agents.

blocks.quote: Summary
Question Answer

What is an agent? An LLM wrapped in an observe→reason→act loop with tools and memory Who invented agents? Classical AI (1950s–1990s) established the paradigm; \cite[Yao et al. (2023)]{yao2023react} made it practical with LLMs How does tool use work? LLM generates structured JSON; orchestrator parses, executes, returns result How do agents remember? Context window (working memory) + external stores (vector DBs, scratchpads) What is ReAct? Interleaving reasoning traces and actions in a single prompt stream What are multi-agent systems? Multiple specialized LLM agents collaborating via an orchestrator What are the risks? Goal misinterpretation, unbounded iteration, prompt injection via tools How does this relate to web search? Web search is a single-tool, single-step agent. Full agents generalize this
